lesson.title: The Doll That Took a Beating: Bandura's Bobo Doll Experiment
lesson.summary: Bandura, Ross, and Ross's 1961 Bobo doll experiment showed that preschoolers would imitate an adult's aggressive behavior toward an inflatable doll purely from observation, becoming one of the most famous demonstrations in the history of psychology.
lesson.body:
By the early 1960s, Bandura wanted direct experimental evidence for the claim at the heart of social learning theory and observational learning: that children could learn a whole pattern of behavior simply by watching an adult model perform it, without any reinforcement of their own. He designed a study using an inflatable, bottom-weighted toy called a Bobo doll, built to wobble and pop back upright when struck.

In the basic procedure, preschool children individually watched an adult model in a room with toys. In the aggressive condition, the model attacked the Bobo doll in specific, distinctive ways: punching it, hitting it with a mallet, kicking it, tossing it in the air, and shouting phrases like 'Sock him' and 'Pow.' In the nonaggressive condition, the model played quietly with other toys and ignored the doll. Afterward, each child was mildly frustrated by being shown attractive toys they were then not allowed to play with, and was placed alone in a room containing the Bobo doll and an assortment of other toys, some aggressive and some not, while observers watched through a one-way mirror.

Children who had watched the aggressive model showed significantly more aggression than children in the nonaggressive or no-model conditions, both toward the doll generally and, notably, in the specific forms they'd witnessed: the same phrases, the same mallet strikes, behaviors those children had never displayed before and had no direct reinforcement for performing themselves. That last detail was the crucial evidence for observational learning: the children weren't just generally more worked up, they were reproducing particular, novel actions they'd only ever seen someone else do.

A 1965 follow-up added a further twist that sharpened Bandura's learning-versus-performance distinction: children watched a model who was either rewarded, punished, or given no consequence for aggression. Children who saw the model punished showed less spontaneous imitation than the others, but when the experimenters later simply offered the children an incentive to reproduce what the model had done, children across all three conditions showed they had learned the aggressive behaviors just as well. Punishment had suppressed performance, not learning itself.

The Bobo doll studies are foundational, still widely taught, and connect directly to the scientific method: they used a controlled experiment with random assignment to conditions and a fairly explicit operational definition of aggression, which is what allows the causal claim that observing the model, not something else about the children, produced the difference in behavior. That said, the studies have also drawn real methodological criticism over the decades, including questions about how much hitting an inflatable doll designed to be struck actually tells us about real-world aggression, whether children in a lab setting were partly just doing what they sensed was expected of them, and how well the findings generalize outside that specific setup. The fair summary is that the Bobo doll study remains a landmark demonstration of observational learning, not a settled, uncontroversial proof about the origins of real-world violence.
